Whose Tickets Are These? →

Applying authorize Per Route

Who's allowed to create a ticket is a different question from who's allowed to change one — the routes say so directly.

authorize (previous slide) reads as a short, declarative statement sitting right in the route definition, the same way validate({...}) does:

// Figure 4.10: different roles for different actions (src/routes/ticket.routes.js, excerpt)
router.post(
  '/',
  authorize('customer'),
  validate({ body: createTicketSchema }),
  ticketController.createTicket,
);

router.patch(
  '/:id',
  authorize('agent', 'admin'),
  validate({ params: ticketIdParamSchema, body: updateTicketSchema }),
  ticketController.updateTicket,
);

Creating a ticket is authorize('customer') only — in this domain, tickets are things customers submit, not something an agent or admin files on someone else's behalf. Changing one — status, reassigning assignedAgentId — is the opposite: authorize('agent', 'admin'), since those are staff actions a customer has no reason to perform directly. GET /tickets and GET /tickets/:id, notice, carry no authorize call at all: every role is allowed to read the ticket list, just each scoped to a different slice of it — which is a different kind of restriction entirely, and the next topic's whole subject.

Order matters here the same way it did for validate stacking multiple schemas (Lesson 3): authorize runs before validate, so a customer without permission gets a 403 immediately, without this project ever spending effort validating a request body it was already going to reject on role grounds alone.
